title: In deed and in truth (1 John 3:18)
hookLine: let us not love in word, but in deed

cards: At their wedding, she said beautiful things. Decades later, nobody remembers the vows word for word.

What the grandchildren remember is that every winter morning, before she left for work, he went out in the cold, scraped the ice off her windshield and started the car so it would be warm. He was not a man of speeches.
He rarely said I love you out loud. He scraped that windshield every icy morning, for decades. John, in his first letter, has been talking about love.
And then he says the thing that windshield was saying.

teach.h: HE LAID DOWN HIS LIFE FOR US.
teach.b: First John sets it up with Christ himself. We know what love is, he says, because Jesus laid down his life for us, and so we ought to lay down our lives for each other. That's the high bar.
Then he brings it straight down to the kitchen table.
The Douay-Rheims: "He that hath the substance of this world, and shall see his brother in need, and shall shut up his bowels from him: how doth the charity of God abide in him?"
Bowels sounds strange now, but the Greek word, splanchna, means your insides, your gut, the place Greek speakers located compassion. In plain English: shut his heart.
You see someone in need, you feel that tug in your gut, and you close the door on it. John asks how God's love could possibly be living there.

teach.h: NOT IN WORD, NOR IN TONGUE.
teach.b: Then the line: "My little children, let us not love in word, nor in tongue, but in deed, and in truth." Two pairs. Not word and tongue: not just talk.

teach.h: DEED, AND TRUTH: HANDS AND HEART.
teach.b: But deed and truth. Deed is the doing.

teach.h: LET US LOVE IN DEED AND IN TRUTH.
teach.b: Truth means the love is real, not a show, not a deed done to be seen. You can do a kind thing for a selfish reason; John wants both the hands and the heart. Notice the tender start: my little children.
He's not scolding. He sounds like a grandfather. In the Catholic tradition, this is the ground of the works of mercy: feeding, clothing, visiting, sheltering.
Love that has a shape you could photograph.

how: Catholics practice love in deed through the corporal works of mercy, such as feeding the hungry, sheltering the homeless and visiting the sick and imprisoned, often through parishes, Catholic charities and groups like the Society of Saint Vincent de Paul.

games.q: you have plenty, and you see someone you know in real need. you feel the tug of compassion. what does John ask?
o: tell them you'll keep them in your thoughts.
open your heart and your hands, in deed and in truth.
point them to someone else who could help.
games.why: John asks how God's love can live in someone who shuts their heart on a brother in need. let us not love in word, nor in tongue, but in deed, and in truth.

practice: Bring to mind someone you love who might not feel it much lately, and picture their ordinary day.

Choose one small, concrete thing that would make it easier, a coffee left on a desk, a chore done before they get to it, a repaired zipper, and picture yourself doing it quietly, without announcing it.
If you pray, offer it to God for them; if not, hold their face and your plan together.
